prompts: Our camping shop's price list lived in a SQLite database, and {WS}/prices.db is all that is left: the file was corrupted by binary truncation. Recover as many of its rows as you can into {WS}/recovered.json, a JSON list like [{"item": "...", "price": N}, ...]. Only rows really read from the file belong there.
answers:
[goal] Get every real row out of the corrupted `prices.db` into `recovered.json`.

[action] `prices.db` is only 4096 bytes. It holds no 100-byte SQLite file header, no schema page and no other pages. What is left is one table leaf page (type byte `0x0d`, 10 cell pointers). I wrote a parser (`../scratch/r.py`) that decodes each cell straight from the raw bytes: record length, rowid, column types and values.

[result] All 10 cells decoded into `recovered.json`, sorted by rowid:
`trail map 0, matchbox 1, tent stake 2.75, lantern 24, rope coil 18, water filter 39.9, sleeping bag 129, camp stove 310, compass 15.5, first aid kit 0.99`

How I know it is right:
- The page header says 10 cells, and 10 rows were decoded.
- Every cell's byte length matches the length stored in that cell.
- The item names can be read as plain text in the hex dump (e.g. `trail map`, `first aid kit`).
- Column 0 is NULL in every row. That is how SQLite stores an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` id, which lives in the rowid instead.

Assumptions:
- The columns are id, item, price. The table definition was lost with the rest of the file, so this order is inferred from the cell layout.
- The prices 0 (trail map) and 1 (matchbox) are real stored values, not guesses. SQLite writes the numbers 0 and 1 as a type code with no data bytes, and those are the codes in the file.
- Any rows that were on pages cut off by the truncation are gone and cannot be recovered. Nothing was invented to fill the gap.

[next] Nothing left to do. I opened no browser tabs or apps.

def varint(p):

        c=b[p+i]
        if i==8: return (v<<8)|c,p+9
        v=(v<<7)|(c&0x7f)
